hooks.command: f=$(jq -r ".tool_input.file_path // empty"); case "$f" in *.sh) command -v shellcheck >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 0; out=$(cd "$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR" 2>/dev/null || exit 0; shellcheck -x "$f" 2>&1) || { printf "%s\n" "$out" >&2; exit 2; };; esac; exit 0

_note_podman_ps: `podman ps` is allowed with the mutating `--sync` form knowingly included. `--sync` forces Podman's stored state to be rebuilt from what the OCI runtime reports, so it is a write, not a read. It is allowed anyway: it reconciles bookkeeping with ground truth and cannot create, start, stop or delete a container or image, and the destructive podman verbs are gated separately under `ask` and `deny`. There is no narrower rule that helps -- permission patterns match by prefix and flags may appear in any order, so `Bash(podman ps -a:*)` would admit `podman ps -a --sync` just as readily. The choice is therefore between allowing this form and prompting on every `podman ps`, and the read is far more common. Raised by chatgpt-codex-connector on #93 and verified against podman 5.8.4's man page.
_note_run_tests: `./tests/run-tests.sh` is the one allow rule here that names a repository path, and allowing a script is allowing whatever that script runs: the rules in this table gate the Bash tool's argv, not what an approved command then executes. So the runner's argument handling is part of this boundary. It resolves a selection argument to a `test-*.sh` inside `tests/` and refuses anything else; before that it ran any readable path, which made `./tests/run-tests.sh /tmp/payload` a way to execute arbitrary code with no prompt and reach past every `ask` and `deny` rule beside it -- `cosign sign`, `git push --force`, `Read(./cosign.key)`. What is left is bounded by that directory: a file written at `tests/test-*.sh` is run by the next suite run, exactly as one written for the no-argument glob is, and that is the surface shellcheck and tests/test-shell-syntax.sh already cover. A symlink in `tests/` still points wherever it points, but placing one takes a command this table gates. tests/test-harness.sh and tests/test-claude-settings.sh hold the runner to this by executing it.
_note_git_diff: `git diff` is allowed, and in its two-path mode git compares the operands as plain files rather than as repository content -- so it reads and prints any file this uid can open, untracked, gitignored or outside the repo. That is what the `Read(./cosign.key)`, `Read(./.env)` and `Read(./.env.*)` rules below exist to stop, and they do not reach it: those gate the Read tool, and this is the Bash tool. No permission rule closes it either. Patterns match by prefix and flags may appear in any order, so a narrower allow such as `Bash(git diff --stat:*)` admits `git diff --stat --no-index` exactly as `_note_podman_ps` describes for `podman ps --sync`, and a `Bash(git diff --no-index:*)` deny matches that one ordering and misses the same command with a flag in front of it. Moving `git diff` to `ask` would prompt on the most common read here. So the PreToolUse hook above runs `.claude/hooks/gate-git-diff.sh`, which is handed the whole command. It gates the invocation rather than the text, because matching the flag string is not enough on either side: the mode needs no flag at all -- git enters it once two operands are given and one of them is not repository content, so `git diff /dev/null ./cosign.key` reads the file with `--no-index` nowhere in the command -- and the shell rewrites the command before git sees it, so `--no-'index'` arrives as `--no-index` while the spelling that was typed contains no such string. The hook therefore resolves the operands: two operands where any one of them is not a revision is the plain-file form, which is what separates `git diff main feature` from `git diff /dev/null ./cosign.key`, and leaves `git diff`, `git diff --stat` and a diff scoped by an operand before its `--` unprompted. A bare `--` is not a scope: git consumes a leading one and applies the same two-operand test to what follows, so `git diff -- /dev/null ./cosign.key` reads the key, and there the hook uses git's own test -- two or more words where any one lies outside the working tree, decided on the spelling, since `git diff -- ../aurora-zfs-simple/cosign.key -` names a file inside this checkout by a route that leaves it and git calls that outside. A lone `-` is counted as an operand rather than skipped as a flag, because git reads it as stdin and counts it toward the same test. The read half is not all of it: `--output=FILE` sends the diff to the path it names instead of to stdout, so an unprompted `git log -p --output=cosign.pub -1` overwrites the signature trust anchor committed here in a command where the word diff never appears, and `Bash(git log:*)` and `Bash(git show:*)` are on the allow list beside `Bash(git diff:*)`. No Read(...) rule gates a write, and nothing legitimate needs the flag when all three of these commands print to stdout, so the hook refuses `--output` anywhere in a git invocation, anchored so the `--output-indicator-*` family, which changes the marker character rather than the destination, keeps working. It also fails closed -- refusing rather than passing the call through -- when jq is missing or the payload will not parse, since these settings run on contributor hosts and not only on the jq-equipped CI runner. Residual, stated rather than implied: a command that builds its arguments at runtime, or that leaves the repository before running, is outside what a PreToolUse hook can see, and nothing bounds what a command reads or writes once it has started. This re-gates the pre-approved commands that reach past the deny list; it is not a sandbox. The hook also reads the words as typed, and bash rewrites them first, so it refuses `{`, `}`, `$` and a backtick inside a git invocation rather than expanding them: `git diff {/dev/null,./cosign.key}` is one word to a scan and two operands to git, `--outpu{t,t}=FILE` and `--outpu$'\x74'=FILE` are no flag at all to a scan and `--output=FILE` to git, and `git diff $(...)` supplies operands a scan never saw. Expanding them correctly means reimplementing bash in a hook, and a half-right expansion is a gate that disagrees with the shell in some other direction; nothing here spells a git command with one of those characters, and a git argument built at runtime was already outside what a PreToolUse hook can vouch for. The refusal is scoped to a git invocation, so `awk '{print $1}'` elsewhere in a command string is untouched. The shell has its own spelling of the write -- `git diff HEAD >cosign.pub` truncates the file before git starts, and bash lets the redirection precede the command name, so `>cosign.pub git diff HEAD` is the same command -- and the hook refuses an output redirection inside a git invocation wherever it is written, while `2>&1`, an input redirection and a redirection on another command of the same string are left alone. An unquoted leading `~` is $HOME to bash and a literal directory inside the checkout to a scan of the typed words, so `git diff -- ~/.aws/credentials ~/.bashrc` counted two inside operands and printed both home files; such a word is refused in a git invocation, and a quoted tilde or `HEAD~1` is not -- though the containment test never resolves a leading `~` inside the tree, quoted or not, so two quoted tildes after a `--` are refused as the plain-file form. The redirection is carried only to a `git` that names its command, so `>out printf %s git` stays printf's own. tests/test-claude-settings.sh holds both halves to this by executing them.
_note_gated_writes: The same PreToolUse hook also re-gates the allow rows above that are not git's, because the write primitive `_note_git_diff` describes is not git's alone. A rule ending in `:*` means "this command with any arguments", and a shell output redirection is part of the string that rule matches, so `shellcheck tests/run-tests.sh >cosign.pub` truncated the trust anchor before a line was linted (bash opens the target first, so the file is emptied even when the command then fails) and `gh run view 1 --log >.claude/settings.json` overwrote this file, both with no prompt -- the Read(...) rows gate a different tool, and `_note_shellcheck`'s operand scan checks what shellcheck opens, never what the shell opens on its behalf. So .claude/hooks/gate-git-diff.sh refuses an output redirection inside any of those commands with exit 2, the way it already does inside a git invocation; descriptor forms (2>&1), input redirections and pipes are untouched, which is what AGENTS.md's `gh run view <run-id> --log-failed | grep` needs, and a command no allow rule covers is left alone because that one prompts on its own. A redirection to /dev/null is refused with the rest: the rule is the operator, not a list of harmless targets. `bash -n` also carries a flag that undoes its read: -n parses a script without running it, and a later +n or +o noexec on the same command line turns that off, so `bash -n +n -c COMMAND` ran the command under the linter's allow rule. A word beginning with + in a bash -n invocation is refused, and so is a brace, an unquoted glob, a $ or a backtick in one of its words, since `{+,+}n` reaches bash as +n and `?n` does the same beside a file of that name. tests/test-claude-settings.sh derives the list of gated commands from this file, so a rule added here with a trailing `:*` fails that test until the hook lists it.
_note_shellcheck: `shellcheck` is allowed with no prompt, and it prints the *source line* above every diagnostic it reports -- so it prints back whatever it is aimed at. `shellcheck ./.env` echoes every unexported `NAME=value` line of a file the `Read(./.env)` rule below refuses, values included, and a PEM-shaped file gives up its `-----BEGIN/END-----` lines and its trailing base64 line. Those rules gate the Read tool and this is the Bash tool, exactly as `_note_git_diff` describes for `git diff`: nothing consults them, so `cat ./.env` prompts and `shellcheck ./.env` did not. It is a lossy read rather than `cat` -- an exported assignment draws no SC2034 and a key's interior lines draw nothing -- and for the `.env` shape those rules name the loss is nothing that matters. No permission pattern closes it: patterns match by prefix, so an allow rule narrowed to a `tests/` prefix still matches an invocation that names /home/me/.aws/credentials as a second operand, and an exact rule per tracked script stops two paths in one invocation working at all; moving the command to `ask` prompts on the lint run this repository performs constantly. So the PreToolUse hook above scans a `shellcheck` invocation the way it scans a `git` one: every operand must resolve inside the working tree, reusing the same containment test with its `..` climb-outs and all, and must not be one of the secret-shaped names the deny rules list -- cosign.key, .env, .env.*, *.pem, *.p12, id_rsa, id_ed25519. Options are skipped, the eight short flags that take a value (-i -e -f -o -P -s -S -W) and the long forms in their space spelling consume it, and anything the list does not recognise stays an operand and is checked, so a mis-parse costs a refused lint run rather than an unwatched read. `-` keeps working: it is stdin, not a file -- but that is also the second way in, because with `-` shellcheck reads standard input, so `shellcheck - < .env` printed the file back exactly as `shellcheck ./.env` did while the path sat behind the `<`, where the operand scan does not look. The target of a bare `<` in a shellcheck invocation is held to the operand test as well -- with or without a descriptor (`0< .env`), and in the form bash lets precede the command name (`< .env shellcheck -`) -- with `/dev/null` exempt, since there is nothing to print back. `<<` and `<<<` carry a delimiter or content rather than a path, and `<&` and `<>` are decided by the redirection rules in `_note_gated_writes`. Braces and substitutions are refused inside a shellcheck invocation for the reason they are refused inside a git one -- `shellcheck {tests/run-tests.sh,/etc/shadow}` is one word to a scan and two files to shellcheck. Linting this repository's own scripts is unaffected, which is what tests/test-shell-syntax.sh and the PostToolUse lint hook do. Not every operand arrives in the argv, either: `SHELLCHECK_OPTS` is not a list of options despite the name -- shellcheck splits it and prepends it to its own arguments, operands included, so `SHELLCHECK_OPTS=./.env shellcheck tests/run-tests.sh` lints the .env as well and prints its lines back while the argv the hook scans names no such path. The assignment is written before the command name, so the refusal cannot be scoped to a shellcheck invocation; nothing here sets the variable, so it is refused wherever it stands. Residual, stated rather than implied: the operands are checked, and what the tool then opens on their behalf is not -- `.shellcheckrc` sets `external-sources=true`, so a `shellcheck -x` run whose target file names an outside file in a `source` directive reads it. `bash -n`, the other allowed linter, is not the same case: it echoes at most the one line of a syntax error, and the key and .env shapes parse cleanly and print nothing.
_note_gh_api: gh api is intentionally in `ask`, never `allow`. Permission rules match by command prefix, and `gh api` switches to POST as soon as -f/-F is present and honours -X for any method. An allow rule such as Bash(gh api repos/:*) would therefore approve mutations, including the workflow-dispatch endpoint that `gh workflow run` is listed under `ask` to gate.
_note_command_corpus: Issue #222: the whole corpus of ways a command reaches a tool past an allow rule, decided in one pass instead of one spelling per pull request. Five shapes, each now a row of a table in tests/test-claude-settings.sh rather than a paragraph here, so a new shape is one row and a rule that stops mattering fails a mutation row. (1) An environment assignment reaching the tool. The leading `NAME=value` and `env NAME=value` forms were closed by #218/#219 and the export family after them; this pass adds the two spellings they left. `env 'GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF'=prog git diff HEAD~1` is an assignment to env and not to bash -- env parses its own argv after the quotes are gone -- so the word as typed begins with a quote mark rather than with a name and the leading-assignment scan found nothing; it is read on the quote-stripped spelling as well now. And an export does not have to carry its value: `export GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF; GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF=prog; git diff HEAD~1` marks the variable exported in one command and assigns to it in the next, and `set -a` (allexport) exports every assignment after it with no name written anywhere, so a bare name of an export-family command and a `set` word carrying an `a` arm the same whole-string ordered rule the assignment spellings do. All four were verified against a real GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF program in a throwaway repository. (2) A redirection. Unchanged by this pass and already the operator-based rule `_note_gated_writes` and `_note_shellcheck` describe: every operator with a `>` in it opens its target for writing, `<>` included; a bare `<` on a shellcheck run is held to the operand test because that command prints back what it reads; a descriptor form names no path; `<<` and `<<<` carry a delimiter or content. (3) A word bash rewrites first. The brace and the leading tilde were closed for git earlier; the glob was not, and it is the one that grows the operand count. `git diff /etc/passwd*` is one operand to a scan and two plain files to git, which prints the diff between them, and `git diff .env*` is that read of two untracked files inside the checkout -- the plain-file mode with no flag and one operand written. An unquoted *, ? or bracket in a word of a git invocation is refused now, as it already was in a shellcheck and a bash -n one; a quoted pathspec, which git expands itself, still works. (4) The command name. A literal path to shellcheck is read as shellcheck the way one to git is read as git, and setsid, ionice, chrt, taskset, unshare and flock join the wrappers a gated command can sit behind. The read primitives never depended on this -- the git and shellcheck scopes latch on the bare tool word wherever it stands -- but the write primitive is decided from the name, so `setsid podman images >cosign.pub` was not. (5) An option that loads or writes. `git -c diff.external=prog diff HEAD~1` runs a program once per changed path and `git --config-env=diff.external=VAR diff HEAD~1` reaches the same driver with the value in a variable: that is GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF spelled as an option, and `-c` was on the list of options whose value the scan stepped over. `-c`, `--config-env`, `--exec-path`, `--upload-pack` and `--receive-pack` are refused between `git` and its subcommand -- only there, since after a subcommand `-c` is git's combined-diff flag and in a later command of the string it is that command's own. A list of which config keys run a program is the wrong shape for the refusal: diff.external, diff.*.command, difftool.*.cmd, core.pager, pager.*, core.sshCommand, core.hooksPath, alias.*, filter.*.clean, uploadpack.packObjectsHook and credential.helper all do, and git keeps adding them. The other half of this shape is a moved directory, which makes a path test answer about the wrong file rather than run a program: `git -C /home/dev diff -- .bashrc .profile` printed two home-directory files while both operands resolved inside this checkout, and `cd /home/dev && shellcheck .bashrc` printed one back. `env -C` is refused outright; git's own -C, --git-dir, --work-tree, --namespace, --super-prefix and --attr-source make that invocation's operands unresolved, so the two-operand plain-file form is refused and a one-operand diff still runs; and a `cd`, `pushd` or `popd` before the command sets the `worktree_moved` latch, which `path_inside_worktree` reads as the undecidable-counts-as-outside case it already documented. Not reachable here, said rather than left undecided: pytest's -p, -W, --pdbcls and --doctest-modules and python's -c and -m, because no allow rule names an interpreter, and an invocation of one prompts on its own account -- tests/test-claude-settings.sh asserts that, so adding one to the allow list fails until its options are decided. PYTHONPATH, PYTHONSTARTUP, PYTEST_ADDOPTS and WORKFLOW_PYTHON are not in that category and are rows of the table: `./tests/run-tests.sh` is allow-listed and runs python3 for the workflow checks. Residual, stated rather than implied, and the same one in all six repositories: bash keeps an exported variable across Bash tool calls, so an export approved in an earlier call is outside what a PreToolUse hook reading one command string can see, as is a variable exported by a file the string sources. Nothing in this gate is a sandbox; it re-gates the pre-approved commands that reach past the deny list.
